convoLines.text: "Can we talk?" Marisol sits down near you. "Just... talk. Like people used to."
"Do you ever — no. Never mind." They don't look away, though. They want you to ask.
"Nice. Sit. The fire's warm."
"It helps. Just — saying it out loud to someone who's actually listening. It helps."
"Short version — Still on that hard time."
They relax, a fraction. This is going well.
"...Fine. This had better be worth it."
"Forget I said anything. What did you want?"
"You want to know about that? Okay." "Robin is gone and Gabriela is gone and the world just... continues. That's the part I can't stand."
"...I need to go be quiet for a while."
They glance at the fire, then back. The quiet doesn't seem to bother them.
"Thanks for... you know. Just listening."
"We gave them a good burial. Doesn't feel like enough, does it?"
"Come get air with me. I need to think out loud."
It's quiet at the ridge. Stella doesn't say much. Sometimes that's the whole point.
"Most days I don't think about it. Today I am. Appreciate you noticing. Not that it matters."
"Robin is gone and Gabriela is gone. The fire doesn't care. That's what gets me — the fire doesn't care."
"I work alone. Nothing personal. ...It's a little personal."
"Sleep's gone strange. I hum one note, over and over, when the dark comes at odd hours now. Whatever gets me to morning."
You show them Wild Ginger — where it grows, how to tell it apart. A short laugh. "And I've been walking past it for weeks."
A warmth settles over the conversation — they lean in a little.
"Anyway." A small smile.
"Yeah? What's up? Could be wrong, though."
"About grief — yeah, we never did get back to that."
"I should go. Before I overthink this conversation too."
A comfortable quiet settles. They smile a little, and let it be.
"This was good." They mean it.
"I keep dreaming about rows of pods. Humming. Tell me I'm not the only one."

"It's my grandmother, Ashley. Was taken. Eighty-one years old and they called her boring. Eighty-one years. The pods get into my sleep some nights. Row on row of them, humming like a held note -- and I wake up reaching for something that isn't there."
"Sorry — I shouldn't load that on you. What's up? No time to waste."
The ground remembers.
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
Something eases in their shoulders. They're really talking to you now.
"Yeah. Sorry. It's -- never mind. Forget I said anything." They look away, embarrassed at having wanted something.
Names, named.
"Okay. That's — I need a minute. A long minute."
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
"The pantry's nearly bare. Will you forage with me tomorrow? Two pairs of eyes, twice the ground."
"Another day like today and we're choosing who eats. I know the ridge above the creek — come with me and we'll fill packs before dark."
There is no playable joint foraging outing yet. Giving food does not perform the promised outing.
"Sorry — I shouldn't load that on you. What's up?"
Found something. Follow it to the moot.
"You're a good listener, you know that?" A tired smile.
They hear the warmth in it. They're not ready to let it in.
"No, yeah, of course. Forget I asked." They won't forget. They'll just stop asking.
Said. At the moot. Let the fire decide what it means.
"I should let you go. Be well, okay?"
"No — you're right, it's a lot. Forget it."
"Right. Well." That's the whole goodbye.
"About what happened to my taken kin — You talk to it -- the System. Have you ever asked? About the taken -- about Ashley?"
"All right. Thank you for telling me."
"...Sorry, lost my train of thought."
"Forget I said anything. What did you want?"
"Huh. Let me think about that." "Huh. I answered that once — back when the answer was simpler." "They took you — The Box, on the screens. The whole fire watched. Nobody knew where to look."
"We'll see what the treeline brings. We always do."
"I do the small things right. The big things notice."
"Still on what's been happening."
"Oh — okay. Later, then."
"Hm. Never mind — go on."
"What's the kindest thing someone's done for you out here?"
"That's the good stuff. Quiet generosity. It's holding this whole thing together."
"There's more, but that's for another fire."
"Someone saved me the last of the stew once. Didn't say anything, just put the bowl down and walked off. I think about that bowl more than I think about the monsters."
A flicker at the corner of their mouth. Not quite a smile. Not quite anything.
A pause that's a beat too long. "I think you're confused," Benoit says, not quite looking at you.
"...What's that supposed to mean?" Their voice goes careful.
"Still on the kindest thing someone's done for you."
"Finally. I was wondering when you'd see my value."
"Okay. We'll pick this up later."
They glance at the fire, then back. The quiet doesn't seem to bother them.
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
"Can I tell you something? Before the scattering, I said something cruel. I think about it every day."
Marisol has an edge today — something curdled.
"So." They look at the fire for a moment.
"...Sorry, lost my train of thought."
"Don't tell anyone I told you. What's on your mind?"
"Still on their secret."
The easy manner evaporates. What's left is watching you back.
A wall comes down, then — surprisingly — a door opens behind it. "I'm not from Denver. I'm from Columbus, Ohio. I was ashamed of the truth. Out here nobody asks, so I stopped telling." Quiet. Real.
"Alright — I should get back to it."
"You're a good listener, you know that?" A tired smile.
"What's something you're good at that nobody here knows about?"
"Noted. Filing that under 'extremely useful.' The village needs that."
"I can do mending. Not well — well enough that nobody's died from it yet. That's my whole résumé now: nobody's died from it yet."
"...Sorry, lost my train of thought."
"Hm. Never mind — go on."
Elena looks at you, level. "I told you the truth. You can keep poking it, but it's told."
"Still on what you're good at, as it were."
"Not right now. I've got my own things to handle."
"That again?" Elena sighs. "I confessed that already. I'm not confessing it twice for dramatic effect."
"We went over this," Elena says, a little tired. "I already told you the truth about that."
They fill the quiet. "Anyway — where was I?"
"Rest when you can. We'll talk again soon."
"...Actually, forget it."
"It's been a while. Glad we circled back to that favor."
"It's quiet today. Wrong kind of quiet."
A long exhale. "I'll get there. Just needed a minute where I didn't have to be fine."
"You want to know about that? Okay." "You asked me that before. It's a different question now." "Mia always took the burnt piece. Said someone had to. I take it now."
Something eases in their shoulders. They're really talking to you now.
"That's the whole of it. Sorry."
"Sure — what's on your mind?"
"Huh. Let me think about that." "You're family now. Chosen family — the kind that actually counts." "Don't make me say it twice."
"Here's what it would take, if you want more than this: show up when it costs you something. That's the whole test."
"Still on each other."
You show them Bitter Leaf — where it grows, how to tell it apart. They nod slowly, committing it to memory. "Good to know. Really good to know."
"I should go. You know where to find me."
A comfortable quiet settles. They smile a little, and let it be.
"It's been a while. Glad we circled back to what's been happening."
They're smiling as you go. "Come back anytime."
"Don't mind me. Today's just heavy."
"Walk with me? I want another pair of eyes on something."
Elena shows you where they go to think. "Don't tell the others. Everyone needs one place."
"I — yeah. It helps, hearing that. That is all."
"I dreamed Mia was still here. Woke up angry at the dream. Stupid."
"Okay. Yeah. I trust you."
"I do push-ups at dawn. It doesn't bring anyone back. It just keeps my hands from shaking."
"Anyway." A small smile.
"Go on, then. I'll be thinking good thoughts at you."
You say nothing. Neither do they, for a while — and it's fine.
"Thanks for... you know. Just listening."
"This was good." They mean it.
